paragraphs.section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > hiNeuroS generation
paragraphs.text: NHF1 fibroblasts were transduced with LV‐RANTES‐IL‐15‐GFP, followed by a cocktail of LV‐Sox2 and LV‐rtTA as previously described. 29 Following transduction, hiNeuroS were generated as previously described. 17 Briefly, cells were cultured in ReNcell NSC maintenance medium (Sigma‐Aldrich) supplemented with epidermal growth factor (epidermal growth factor [EGF]; 20 ng/mL, Gemini Bio‐Products), fibroblast growth factor (fibroblast growth factor [FGF]; 20 ng/mL, Sigma‐Aldrich), and doxycycline (2 μg/mL, Sigma‐Aldrich). EGF, FGF, and doxycycline were replenished every other day. Newly formed spheres were collected and seeded on pre‐coated laminin (10 mg/mL, Sigma‐Aldrich) plates. The next day, nonadherent cells were washed away and new spheres were allowed to regenerate from the remaining attached cells. This process of laminin selection was completed in triplicate. Following laminin selection, hiNeuroS were maintained in low attachment Nunclon Sphera (Thermo Scientific) flasks to promote sphere formation and expansion.

paragraphs.section: RESULTS > Generation and characterization of iNSCs expressing RANTES/IL‐15
paragraphs.text: Engineered iNSCs possess great potential for cell therapy applications due to their innate tumor‐homing and ability to provide sustained delivery of biologic agents. To investigate whether these unique properties of iNSCs can enhance anti‐tumor properties of CAR‐T cells, we first constructed a lentiviral vector (LV) encoding human RANTES and IL‐15 (Figure 2a). In this construct, RANTES and IL‐15 were cloned under control of the EF‐1 alpha promoter and separated by a 2A‐peptide sequence. An IRES element driving green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression was also included to quantify transduction efficiency. Using our well‐established methodology for converting human fibroblasts into second‐generation iNSCs, human‐induced neurospheres (hiNeuroS), 17 we engineered RANTES/IL‐15‐secreting hiNeuroS (hiNeuroSRANTES‐IL‐15) (Figure 2b). Robust expression of the GFP reporter gene was detected by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2c). ELISA analysis of conditioned media confirmed RANTES/IL‐15 secretion, with hiNeuroSRANTES‐IL‐15 producing 12,777 pg/mL of RANTES and 1377 pg/mL of IL‐15 over 72 h (Figure 2d).

paragraphs.section: RESULTS > Investigating the impact of cell‐based RANTES/IL‐15 delivery on CAR‐T‐cell therapy in GBM
paragraphs.text: To begin investigating cell‐based delivery of RANTES/IL‐15 to enhance CAR‐T‐cell migration and proliferation, we first transduced human U87 GBM cells with a replication‐incompetent retroviral vector (RV) encoding human RANTES and IL‐15 (U87RANTES‐IL‐15). Enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis of conditioned media confirmed cytokine expression, with U87RANTES‐IL‐15 cells producing 7721 pg/mL of RANTES and 150 pg/mL of IL‐15 over 72 h (Figure 1a). We then performed cell migration and proliferation assays using CAR‐T cells targeting chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 antigen (CSPG4‐CAR‐T) that we previously identified as a clinically relevant target in GBM. 16 T‐cell expression of CSPG4‐CAR was confirmed via flow cytometry (Figure S1). Using a transwell assay system, U87 cells were seeded and cultured overnight in growth medium. The next day, T cells were seeded in transwell inserts, allowed to migrate for 5 h, and enumerated via flow cytometry. We found that U87RANTES‐IL‐15 increased the migration of control T cells 1.9% at 24 h or 6.6% at 48 h, compared to migration toward control U87 cells (Figure 1b,c). This effect was more pronounced in CSPG4‐CAR‐T cells, with migration increasing 8.8% at 24 h or 9.6% at 48 h.

paragraphs.section: RESULTS > Investigating the impact of cell‐based RANTES/IL‐15 delivery on CAR‐T‐cell therapy in GBM
paragraphs.text: To investigate the impact of RANTES/IL‐15 on T‐cell migration in vivo, we implanted U87RANTES‐IL‐15 or control U87 cells into brains of immunodeficient NOD.Cg‐Prkdc scid Il2rg tm1Wjl /SzJ (NSG) mice, which display severe defects in innate and adaptive immunity. Five days later, CSPG4‐CAR‐T cells were infused intravenously (Figure 1d). One, 4, or 7 days after CSPG4‐CAR‐T‐cell infusion, brains were harvested, bisected along the interhemispheric fissure, and separated into “tumor” and “contralateral” (nontumor) hemispheres. We then utilized flow cytometry to quantify number of T cells present within each hemisphere. Using this approach, we found that RANTES/IL‐15 secretion significantly increased the amount of T cells present within tumors, with T‐cell accumulation threefold higher in U87RANTES‐IL‐15 compared to control U87 cells on Day 4 (314 cells/μL, U87RANTES‐IL‐15; 113 cells/μL, U87) and over fourfold higher on Day 7 (133 cells/μL, U87RANTES‐IL‐15; 39 cells/μL, U87; Figure 1e). In contrast, we detected only slight differences in T‐cell accumulation between the contralateral hemispheres on Day 7 (16 cells/μL, U87RANTES‐IL‐15; 5 cells/μL, U87). Taken together, these data demonstrate a proof of concept that RANTES/IL‐15 enhance T‐cell migration in vitro and in vivo. In addition, T‐cell migration into the brain is selective toward the tumor hemisphere with few cells observed in the contralateral hemisphere.

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: The conventional therapies used for treating GBM patients include surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, with about two years of median survival. The treatment of GBM is maximal safe surgical resection followed by radiotherapy with concomitant daily Temozolomide and a further six cycles of maintenance Temozolomide. There are no randomized clinical trials to determine the extent of surgery and specifically investigate its survival benefit in the recurrent setting [3]. Radiotherapy remains a vital modality to improve both local control and survival. This approach has some disadvantages, such as the possibility of injury to the surrounding normal tissue and low-dose delivery to tumor cells away from the radiation site, which could lead to resistance [4]. Temozolomide also could cause toxicity, especially during the adjuvant therapy period. Besides, only patients with O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation are likely to benefit more from the drug. Most patients experience recurrence within six months after standard concurrent chemoradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy [3].

paragraphs.section: Material and methods > Viral vectors and reagents
paragraphs.text: The CD suicide gene and has-miR-34a-5p were synthesized and cloned in a pCDH-GFP-Puro vector to prepare the lentiviral construct containing these genes. pMD2.G and psPAX2 lentivectors were purchased from System Bioscience. 5-Fluorocytosine for in vivo and in vitro experiments were purchased from Alfa Aesar (England).

paragraphs.section: Material and methods > Apoptosis assay
paragraphs.text: GBM cells were seeded onto a 6-well plate at a confluency of 1.5 × 105 cells/well and assigned to three groups of U87MG transduced with miR-34a CD/miR-34a, CD, and the scrambled control. After overnight incubation, CD and CD/miR-34a-expressing cells were treated with 150 μg/ml of 5FC every 24 h. After 72 h, cells were prepared by Annexin V- phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and 7-minoactinomycin D (7-AAD) apoptosis kit (BD Biosciences).

paragraphs.section: Results > Histological analysis
paragraphs.text: H&E staining indicated a typical anaplastic Glioma with increased cell number and mitotic activity in the tumor mass of the control group (scrambled C6 cells, Fig. 4F), which showed high cellularity and atypical changes in nuclei. The size of the tumor, cell number, and the atypical changes in nuclei were significantly decreased in miR-34a-transduced C6 tumor cells (Fig. 4G) compared to scrambled C6 cells. Tumor cells transduced with CD/miR-34a and treated daily with 5FC had no tumor area or, if present, a minimal area with minimal cellularity and scar-like necrotic margins (Fig. 4H).

paragraphs.section: Material and methods > Lentivirus production and cell infection
paragraphs.text: Briefly, the plasmid carrying the CD suicide gene, CD/miR-34a, miR-34a, and the packaging plasmids (psPAX2, pMD2.G) were co-transfected into HEK 293T cells using polyethyleneimine (Polysciences, USA). The cell supernatant containing lentivirus was collected every 12 h for 72 h. The supernatants were centrifuged at 1500 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C to remove cell debris, filter sterilized (0.2 μm filters), and stored at −80 °C until transduction. Then, rat C6 cell line or U87MG Glioma cells were transduced with proper lentivirus vectors. Since all vectors were positive for Green fluorescent protein (GFP), fluorescent microscopy indicates the efficiency of transduction.

paragraphs.section: Results > Cell-cycle assay
paragraphs.text: The number of cells in the G0+G1, S, and G2 phases was significantly different in the U87MG cell line transduced with CD/miR-34a lentivirus, which received 5-FC compared to U87MG cells transduced with scrambled lentivirus. The flow cytometry results showed an increase in the G0+G1 phase by 22.28 % and a decrease of 18.27 % and 6.81 % in the S and G2 phases, respectively. The U87MG cell line transduced with miR-34a lentivirus revealed a significant decrease in the S phase (5.07 %) compared to the U87MG cell line transduced with scrambled lentivirus. The U87MG cells expressing CD plus 5FC alone demonstrated a significant increase in the G0+G1 phase by 22.04 % and a decrease of 12.82 % in the G2 phase compared to the scrambled control (Fig. 3C and D).

paragraphs.section: Material and methods > Cell-cycle assay
paragraphs.text: The cell cycle was evaluated by flow cytometry. GBM cells were seeded onto a 6-well plate (1.5 × 105 cells/well). Cells were divided into three cell groups, namely U87MG cells transduced with miR-34a, cells transduced with CD/miR-34a, cells transduced with CD, and the scrambled control. After overnight incubation, CD and CD/miR-34a-expressing cells were treated with 150 μg/ml of 5FC every 24 h. Cells were collected, washed with PBS, transferred to a new tube of cold 70 % ethanol dropwise on vortex, and retained at −20 °C for 24 h. After the removal of ethanol by centrifugation, cells were rinsed with PBS. The pellets were dissolved in a solution containing 200 μl of propidium iodide (50 μg/ml) (Sigma), RNase (1 mg/ml) (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and Triton X-100 (Sigma) and incubated for 40 min at 37 °C in the dark. The cell cycle was evaluated by flow cytometry.

paragraphs.text: The overexpression of miR-34a in U87MG and C6 cells was analyzed using qRT-PCR, and the fold increases in the expression levels were 38 and 146.5, respectively, compared to the control group (Fig. 2C). paragraphs.section: Material and methods > Implantation of C6 Glioma cells
paragraphs.text: Male Wistar rats weighing 200–250 g were anesthetized (100 mg/kg Ketamine and 5 mg/kg Xylazine), and C6 Glioma cells (1 × 106 cells in 10 μl of PBS) were stereotactically implanted into the right dorsolateral striatum (anterior 0.24 mm; lateral 3.4 mm; lateral depth 3.3 mm, according to the bregma). Rats were assigned to four groups. The control group received PBS; the scrambled control group received SNORD-transduced C6 cells, the miR-34a group received miR-34a-transduced C6 cells, and the CD/miR-34a group received CD/miR-34a-transduced C6 cells with 5FC treatment groups (each group contained four rats). One day after surgery, a group of rats implanted by transduced C6 cells received subcutaneous injections of 5-FC (30 mg/kg) daily for two weeks. The dose of 5FC was calculated based on the IC50 value; the drug was injected subcutaneously into the neck to reduce the dose and increase the drug release time. Twenty-eight days after cell implantation, the animals were euthanized. The results of the in vitro tests revealed that the cell proliferation inhibition and apoptotic induction of CD+5FC alone were equivalent to or less than those obtained from miR-34a, so we did not conduct the in vivo parts of this treatment.

paragraphs.section: Discussion
paragraphs.text: Despite promising results from both in vitro and in vivo experiments, there are some issues regarding CD/miR-34a gene therapy in patients with GBM. In this study, the C6 cell line was first transduced with CD/miR-34a and then administered to the brains of rats to induce a murine model of GBM and assess the therapeutic effect of CD/miR-34a. For the successful delivery of the miR-34a/CD suicide gene to the brain tumor cells of patients, an effective administration route is required. Recent research applied different vehicles for gene delivery of the CD suicide gene, such as viral vectors [29,60,61] and mesenchymal stem cells [28,62,63]. Using a lentiviral delivery system leads to the transduction of all kinds of cells, including tumor cells and the normal cells of the same tissue or even normal cells of other tissues exposed to the vector. Specific targeting of suicide gene therapies along with other therapeutical agents such as miRNAs will lower side effects and increase the therapeutic efficacy. The desired suicide gene expression, controlled by a tissue-specific cellular promoter, provides transcriptional targeting. This method was used against Glioma by developing a baculoviral vector containing the herpes simplex thymidine kinase gene, miR-31, miR127, and miR-143 [64]. In a similar study, HSVtk gene expression was enhanced in GBM cells by specific control of Epo enhancer responds to the core tumor low-oxygen concentration and elevates gene expression along with Nestin intron 2 (NI2), which increases gene expression in neural stem cells or GBM [65].

paragraphs.section: Methods > Production of lentiviral vectors
paragraphs.text: HEK 293 T cells (ATCC, # CRL-3216) were cultured in 10-cm dishes and transfected at a density of 6 × 105 cells/mL. Transfection used PEI complexes containing VSV-G (3.5 µg), GagPol (5.5 µg), Rev (2.5 µg), and the transfer vector MK005-A (10 µg; encoding the CARs). Lentiviral supernatants were collected 48 h after transfection, passed through a 0.45 µm filter, and concentrated by centrifugation for 2 h at 50,000 g. Lentiviral vector titers (TU/mL) were determined by serial dilution, and the percentage of CAR-positive cells was measured by flow cytometry 7 days post-transduction.

paragraphs.section: Results > Evidence of preliminary therapeutic benefit of IL-13Rα2 allogeneic UCAR-T cell intrathecal administration in a patient context
paragraphs.text: Patients MT026-001 to MT026-005 survived 7.6, 17.2, 8.3, 10.5 and 5.7 months, respectively, after the first MT026 infusion, with a median OS of 8.3 months (95 % CI, 6.7-9.8), a maximum survival of 17.2 months, and a 12-month OS rate of 20.0% (95 % CI, 3.5-100 %). When survival was calculated from the time of recurrence, the same patients survived 12.8, 33.2, 9.2, 13.7, and 13.1 months, respectively, yielding a median overall survival of 13.1 months (95 % CI, 12.6-13.6) and a 12-month overall survival rate of 80% (95 % CI, 51.6-100 %). The longest survival was 33.2 months for Patient MT026-002 (Table 1). Survival in these high-grade patients with glioma appeared numerically better than the expected poor median overall survival of ~6–8 months following recurrence4, although comparisons across studies were limited. Mean progression-free survival was 5.6 months (95 % CI: 3.1-8.2), with a maximum of 7.9 months, and the 6-month progression-free survival rate was 40.0 % (95 % CI: 11.8-76.9 %). Two of the five patients (MT026-002 and MT026-003) subsequently received additional investigational CAR-T cell therapies as part of subsequent treatment, as indicated in Fig. 4c. Patient MT026-002 received two administrations of B7H3 targeted CAR-T cells and one administration of HER2 targeted CAR-T cells, whereas Patient MT026-003 received one administration each of B7H3 and EGFR targeted CAR-T cells.

paragraphs.section: Discussion
paragraphs.text: The study design incorporated the following features to overcome barriers and improve patient benefit: (1) use of “off-the-shelf” allogeneic CAR-T cells to avoid long generation time and to circumvent failed autologous T-cell generation from patient donors with secondary T-cell exhaustion; 2) use of the intrathecal route via lumbar puncture instead of intracavity injection to allow exposure of CAR-T cells to newly seeding lesions, given that multifocal gliomas account for 17.2% of all gliomas32; (3) use of intrathecal delivery via lumbar puncture instead of the intraventricular route to improve ease of administration, as drug distribution in CSF via intraventricular or intrathecal routes is similar 4-6 h after administration33; 4) use of monthly rather than weekly dosing to reduce patient burden in clinic settings; and (5) elimination of lymphodepletion. Preconditioning with lymphodepleting agents may create a “favorable” environment for expansion and survival of CAR-T cells in the body by eliminating regulatory T cells; however, this step is used primarily in intravenous CAR-T cell therapy. There is still controversy over whether CAR-T will produce different effects after lymphodepleting chemotherapy in solid tumors. The pre-conditioning with lymphodepleting chemotherapy is not necessary for a local route of administration; it remains uncertain whether lymphodepleting chemotherapy is necessary34,35.

paragraphs.section: Discussion
paragraphs.text: As previously reported, when survival was calculated from the first MT026 infusion, the OS of the five enrolled patients ranged from 5.7 to 17.2 months, with a 12-month OS rate of 20.0 % (95 % CI, 3.5-100 %). When calculated from the time of recurrence, the same patients survived 9.2 to 33.2 months, with a 12-month overall survival rate of 80 % (95 % CI, 51.6-100 %). Although these values appear numerically superior to the epidemiologically reported median OS of 6-8 months for recurrent high-grade glioma, interpretation of the potential survival benefit attributable to MT026 is limited by several factors. First, most observed responses were short-lived: Patient MT026-003 exhibited loss of IL-13Rα2 expression after re-biopsy, suggesting immune escape due to target loss; Patient MT026-004 discontinued MT026 after only four infusions for personal reasons; and Patient MT026-005 experienced highly aggressive tumor growth, with progression occurring within 33 days post-surgery, likely reflecting extreme tumor kinetics and suboptimal dosing frequency. Second, the limited sample size and the fact that two of the five patients received additional investigational UCAR-T therapies targeting other antigens further confound interpretation. Despite these limitations, the clinical data provide preliminary efficacy signals, including tumor responses and potential survival benefit, supporting the need for larger-scale, randomized controlled trials to more definitively determine the therapeutic impact of MT026 in this patient population.

paragraphs.section: Methods > Manufacturing of cell products
paragraphs.text: The IL-13Rα2 CAR sequence (WO/2014/072888, Pfizer INC.) was cloned into the lentiviral vector backbone. T cells collected from healthy donors were enriched by magnetic separation using anti-CD4 and anti-CD8 microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec), and activated with T Cell TransAct (Miltenyi Biotec). At 24 h after activation, lentivirus was mixed with T cells at a final MOI of 3 in 6-well round-bottom plates. For each well, 5 × 106 T cells were combined with medium containing lentivirus (1 × 109 TU/mL) in 15 μL and then spinfected at 800 × g for 60 min. Cells from the same condition were pooled and seeded at 5×105 cells/mL in culture flasks. Two days post-transduction, cells were collected and pelleted for nucleofection of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to generate TCR and HLA-I knockouts. sgRNA for the HLA-I α chain: 5′-CTGACCATGAAGCCACCCTG-3′; sgRNA for TRAC: 5-AGAGTCTCTCAGCTGGTACA-3′; sgRNA for B2M: 5-GAGTAGCGCGAGCACAGCTA-3′. RNPs for each target locus were complexed separately at a 2.5:1 sgRNA (GenScript Biotech): SpCas9 (Thermo) ratio. The two RNPs were then combined to 42 pmol TRAC RNP and 42 pmol HLA-I RNP per million cells. The RNP mixture was diluted in P3 solution (Lonza) and mixed with the cell pellet, then nucleofected using the EO115 program (Lonza). Nucleofected cells were seeded at 1 × 106 cells/ mL. Magnetic separation using anti-CD3 microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec) was performed to remove CD3+ cells and improve the purity of allogeneic universal CAR-T cells. T cells were cultured in X-VIVO 15 medium (Lonza) supplemented with 5% CTS Immune Cell Serum Replacement (Gibco), recombinant human IL-2 (200 U/mL), IL-7 (10 ng/mL), and IL-15 (5 ng/mL) for 14 days. Cell products were stored in cryoprotectant after harvest.

paragraphs.section: Discussion
paragraphs.text: Recent studies have investigated CAR T cell therapies for recurrent glioblastoma and other high-grade gliomas, reporting both promising signals and ongoing challenges. Choi et al. (NEJM, 2024) reported rapid, transient tumor regression using CARv3-TEAM-E cells targeting EGFRvIII and wild-type EGFR via intraventricular infusion28. Bagley et al. (Nat Med, 2024) evaluated intrathecally delivered bivalent CAR T cells targeting EGFR and IL-13Rα2, demonstrating preliminary safety and bioactivity with early radiographic changes but no confirmed objective responses29. Brown et al. (Nat Med, 2024) conducted a phase 1 trial of locoregional IL-13Rα2–targeted CAR T cells in 65 patients, showing acceptable safety and clinical activity, with stable disease or better in 50% of patients but limited median overall survival30. This dual-editing strategy in MT026 eliminates TCR-mediated GvHD and reduces HvGR, providing a potential off-the-shelf therapeutic option (Fig. 5). Although these cells, similar to those generated by the existing B2M knockout strategy, still could not evade rejection by NK cells, this approach demonstrated antitumor activity with reduced alloreactivity in both in vitro and in vivo tumor mouse models via multiplex CRISPR technology. paragraphs.section: Methods > In vitro CAR T Cell Killing assay
paragraphs.text: UCAR-T cells and control cells (Mock-T) were co-cultured at different ratios with the U251 cell lines (Cat# BFN608006387) which were purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Science (Shanghai, China) for 24 h. The U251 cell lines were pre-labeled with CellTrace™ Violet, and post-co-culture cell viability was assessed by PI staining. Flow cytometry was performed to quantify dead target cells, and the percentages of specific CAR-T killing were calculated using the formula: (Dead target cells% -Spontaneous dead target cells %) / (100- Spontaneous dead target cells %) x 100.

paragraphs.section: Introduction
paragraphs.text: Here, we successfully generated MT026 by knocking out TRAC and disrupting HLA-I α chains, enabling control of GvHD and mitigation of HvGR. We present an alternative research approach and show that disruption of most HLA class I molecules enhances the persistence of IL-13Rα2-specific allogeneic CAR-T cells in patients with recurrent glioblastoma. Data from a first-in-human, single-center, open-label investigator-initiated trial (IIT; ChiCTR2000028801) using CRISPR-Cas9–edited universal CAR-T therapy, delivered intrathecally to tumor sites, demonstrated favorable tolerability, safety, pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics, and preliminary efficacy of IL-13Rα2-targeted allogeneic UCAR-T therapy.

paragraphs.section: Methods > End points
paragraphs.text: The primary endpoint was the occurrence and severity of adverse events among all patients who received at least one dose of MT026. Secondary end points included overall survival, progression-free survival, objective response rate, duration of response, disease control rate, and pharmacokinetic parameters. Exploratory endpoints were PK characteristics (CAR DNA copies), changes in pharmacodynamic (PD) parameters (cytokines, lymphocyte count, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio), and relationships between demographic stratification variables (sex, KPS, IL-13Rα2 antigen expression level, IDH1/2 mutation, and MGMT promoter methylation) and response. Adverse events were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0 (NCI CTCAE 5.0). All efficacy endpoints were evaluated according to iRANO criteria for CNS tumors.

paragraphs.section: Results > Evaluation of the effects of HLA-TRAC dual-editing strategy on TCR and HLA-I functions
paragraphs.text: To verify the protective role of the HLA-I gene-editing strategy, we used allogeneic NK cells with IL-2 to enhance NK function. UCAR-T cells were co-cultured with NK cells for 24 h. Only 20–30 % of UCAR-T cells were lysed by NK cells, whereas the positive-control cell line K562, which lacks HLA-I expression, exhibited ~60 % lysis. As expected, WT T cells with HLA-I expression resisted killing (Fig. 1c). In order to further evaluate whether the dual knockout allogeneic UCAR-T cells would induce GvHD on recipients as well as HvGR, which were the common issues of allogeneic UCAR-T cells, UCAR-T generated by different knockout strategies were challenged by allogeneic PBMCs. MT026 cells (TCR-knockout UCAR-T) showed no proliferation when co-cultured with allogeneic PBMCs, in stark contrast to conventional CAR-T cells (TCR-intact) and WT T cells, which exhibited significant activation and expansion (Fig. 1d).

paragraphs.section: Results > IL-13Rα2 allogeneic UCAR-T cells potently inhibit glioma growth in vitro and in vivo
paragraphs.text: The survival curve of the PDOX model indicated that IL-13Rα2 allogeneic UCAR-T therapy suppressed tumor progression in vivo and improved survival, whereas mice in the no-treatment control (NT) group exhibited continuous tumor proliferation, resulting in death from day 30 onward (Fig. 2e). Brain tumor growth was significantly suppressed for 7 days after intratumoral injection of IL-13Rα2 allogeneic UCAR-T cells; however, slight tumor recurrence was observed since 14th day after injection (day 29 after model initiation) (Fig. 2f). Quantitative analysis of BLI in PDOX mice was consistent with survival results: the control group showed a substantial increase in bioluminescence, whereas the experimental group exhibited only a minimal increase (Fig. 2g). Taken together, the in vitro and in vivo data indicate that IL-13Rα2 allogeneic UCAR-T therapy effectively inhibits tumor growth and confers sustained tumor suppression in model animals.

paragraphs.section: Methods > Off-target analysis
paragraphs.text: To assess CRISPR-Cas9 off-target activity, multiple sequencing methods were employed. In AID-seq, genomic DNA from unedited T cells was fragmented, ligated to hairpin adapters, and digested with exonucleases to reduce false positives. Cleavage by Cas9 ribonucleoprotein exposed ends for biotinylated adapter ligation, followed by streptavidin enrichment, nested PCR, and alignment to identify on- and off-target sites. GUIDE-seq and iGUIDE-seq utilized dsODN tags integrated via NHEJ to mark cleavage sites in living T cells. iGUIDE-seq employed a longer dsODN for improved precision. Tagged DNA was fragmented, adapter-ligated, and PCR-amplified before sequencing and alignment. PEM-seq involved shearing DNA, PCR extension with biotinylated primers, and dual barcoding before high-throughput sequencing and analysis via PEM-Q. For editing efficiency, amplicon sequencing of target regions was performed, followed by CRISPResso analysis for quality control, alignment, and indel characterization. All methods enabled comprehensive profiling of CRISPR-induced on- and off-target edits.

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cells Eradicate Tumor Burden and Prolong Survival in an Orthotopic DHG Mouse Model With H3G34R Mutation
paragraphs.text: To further strengthen the translational relevance and robustness of our findings, we performed a repeat in vivo experiment using a more aggressive SJ-HGGX42 model, which has a median survival of 50 days. Additionally, CAR T cells are administered at a later time point (3 weeks postimplantation), when tumors are more established. This design mimics advanced disease with a higher tumor burden, which is clinically more challenging to treat. Importantly, even under these conditions, B7-H3 CAR T cell therapy resulted in tumor clearance in the majority of treated mice, with long-term survival observed compared to CD19 CAR T control mice at the end of the study (Figure S15A–C). To evaluate potential systemic toxicity and cytokine release associated with CAR T cell therapy, we performed multiplex serum cytokine profiling at the end of the experiment, which revealed elevations of IL-6 and IL-8, consistent with CAR T cell activation, without significant increases in IFN-γ, TNF-α, or IL-10. These findings suggest an absence of severe cytokine release or systemic toxicity (Figure S15D). Notably, serum was collected after tumor clearance, which may account for the lack of significant elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are among the most lethal primary brain tumors and represent the leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children and adolescents.1 These tumors are biologically and clinically heterogeneous and are now stratified into molecular subgroups based on recurrent driver mutations in Histone H3.3 (H3.3A) or Histone H3.1 (H3C2).2–4 Approximately 50%-60% of pHGGs harbor mutually exclusive somatic point mutations, such as the presence of methionine at amino acid 27 instead of lysine (K27M) or the presence of arginine or valine at amino acid 34 instead of glycine (G34R/V) within the histone H3 tail.5–7 Pediatric high-grade gliomas with H3K27M mutation, characterized as diffuse midline glioma (DMG), typically arise in midline brain structures, such as the pons, thalamus, or spinal cord, and predominantly affect young children. In contrast, pHGGs with H3G34R/V mutation are classified as diffuse hemispheric glioma (DHG) and are usually located in the cerebral hemispheres, particularly the cortex and subcortical white matter, and occur more frequently in adolescents and young adults.2,6,8,9 These recurrent somatic mutations disrupt local chromatin structure and transcriptional regulation, promoting epigenetic reprogramming and oncogenesis. Despite aggressive multimodal therapy, including maximal surgical resection, radiation, and chemotherapy, DHGs remain uniformly fatal, with a median survival of 12-18 months and 5-year survival rates below 20%.8–10 Unlike their DMG counterparts, DHG remain understudied, and currently, no targeted or immunotherapeutic approaches are approved for these patients, highlighting a critical and unmet need for innovative therapeutic strategies.

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cells Eradicate Tumor Burden and Prolong Survival in an Orthotopic DHG Mouse Model With H3G34R Mutation
paragraphs.text: After B7-H3 CAR T cells’ efficient and specific cytotoxic effect against B7-H3 positive DHG cell lines in vitro, we evaluated their antitumor efficacy in vivo. First, we established an orthotopic xenograft model using SJ-HGGX42 cells implanted intracranially in the cortex of NSG mice. Following confirmation of tumor engraftment via bioluminescence imaging (BLI), mice were randomized into B7-H3 CAR or CD19 CAR treatment arms and administered CAR T cell therapy intratumorally on day 8 postimplantation (Figure 5A). Longitudinal BLI revealed a striking and sustained reduction in tumor burden of B7-H3 CAR T cell-treated mice, whereas CD19 CAR-treated controls exhibited progressive tumor growth (Figure 5B and C). Quantitative analysis of total flux confirmed a significant decline in tumor signal in the B7-H3 CAR cohort, beginning shortly after treatment and sustaining through 300 days (Figure 5C and D). Survival analysis demonstrated a significant survival advantage in B7-H3 CAR T cell-treated mice compared to CD19 CAR controls. The median survival for CD19 CAR-treated mice was 136 days, whereas a median survival was not reached in the B7-H3 CAR T cell-treated cohort (n = 9), with 4 mice remaining alive beyond 300 days at the time of study termination (P = .0004; Figure 5D). H&E staining of brains revealed the absence of tumor in B7-H3 CAR T cell-treated mice, while the control mice had highly dense and diffuse tumoral growth (Figure 5E, Figure S12). Immunohistochemistry confirmed the absence of B7-H3 and H3G34R staining in the B7-H3 CAR T celll-treated group, accompanied by near-complete ablation of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Figure 5E and F, Figure S12). To evaluate potential neurotoxicity and treatment-associated inflammation, we performed IHC for Iba1 on brain sections from CD19 CAR and B7-H3 CAR-treated mice. Quantitative analysis revealed a significant reduction in Iba1+ cells in B7-H3 CAR-treated animals (Figure S13), consistent with decreased microglial activation following effective tumor clearance. Additionally, we utilized multiplex immunofluorescence imaging in CD19 CAR and B7-H3 CAR-treated mice brains to analyze tumor, microglial, and T-cell markers in SJ-HGGX42 tumors following CAR-T treatment. CD19 CAR-T-treated mice showed invasive tumor regions (Vimentin+), proliferating tumor cells (Ki67+), microglia (Iba1+), whereas B7-H3 CAR-T-treated mice brain displayed absence of tumor related phenotype with minimal expression of Iba1+, Vimentin+ and Ki67+ (Figure 5G and H, Figure S14). Analysis of T-cell markers (CD3e and CD8) in CD19- and B7-H3 CAR T cell-treated mice revealed an absence of detectable T cells at the time point analyzed, suggesting either limited persistence or clearance of infused CAR T cells.

paragraphs.section: Methods > IHC Staining of the Mouse Brains
paragraphs.text: Mice were euthanized at experimental end-time points and were perfused with PBS, then with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Brain tissues were coronally sliced into 2, placed cut sections facing downward in the cassettes, and processed for paraffin embedding (see Supplementary Material S1 for details).

paragraphs.section: Methods > Cytotoxicity Assay
paragraphs.text: Cytotoxic efficacy of B7-H3 CAR-T cells was assessed using different detection systems. Tumor cells were CFSE-labeled and plated in a 96-well plate in triplicate and incubated for a minimum of 2 h at 37°C, 5% CO2. Effector cells (mock T, CD19 CAR-T, and B7-H3 CAR-T) were added at desired ratios in the same plate and incubated for 72 h (see Supplementary Material S1 for details).

paragraphs.section: Methods > Cytokine Secretion Analysis
paragraphs.text: KNS42, SJ-HGGX42, and KNS42 B7-H3KO cells were cocultured with effector cells (mock T cells or B7-H3 CAR T cells) at an E:T of 1:1 in triplicate wells of a 96-well plate for 24 h. Then, the plate was centrifuged briefly to let the cells settle down. Culture media was collected and aliquoted in a fresh 96-well plate and frozen at −80°C until used for analysis (see Supplementary Material S1 for details).

paragraphs.section: Methods > Animal Studies
paragraphs.text: All the mouse experiments were performed in accordance with the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC). Male and female NSG (NOD-scid IL2Rgammanull) mice aged 8-12 weeks were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. Tumor cells were intracranially transplanted by drilling a burr hole on the skull at 2.5 mm posterior, then 2.0 mm mediolateral to the bregma; 1 × 106 KNS42 and 1.5 × 106 SJ-HGGX42 cells expressing luciferase were resuspended in 4 μL of phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and were injected in 1 μL increments at 3.5 mm, 2.5 mm, and 2 μL in 1.5 mm from the depth of burr hole (see Supplementary Material S1 for details).

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cells Activation, Exhaustion, and Cytokine Profiles Following Co-culture With DHG Cell Lines (KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42)
paragraphs.text: We evaluated CAR T cell activation and effector cytokine production following 24-h coculture of B7-H3 CAR T cells with DHG cell lines KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42 using a bead-based 13-plex cytokine detection kit employing a flow cytometer. B7-H3 CAR T cells secreted significantly higher levels of IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, Granzyme A, Granzyme B, Perforin, IL-10, IL-17A, IL-4, sFas, sFasL, and Granulysin compared to mock T cells (Figure 3F, Figure S8). These findings confirm that B7-H3 CAR T cells undergo robust antigen-specific activation and mount a strong effector cytokine response upon engagement with DHG tumor targets. We also checked the status of T cell exhaustion after exposure of mock and CAR T cells to the target antigen in KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42 cell lines. After antigen stimulation, B7-H3 CAR T cells displayed significantly higher surface expression of PD1, TIM3, and LAG3 in both DHG models than mock T cells (Figure 3G), consistent with activation-induced exhaustion. These results demonstrate that B7-H3 CAR T cells are capable of robust, dose-dependent cytotoxicity and effector cytokine release upon target recognition, indicative of potent, but sustained T cell activation in the DHG microenvironment.

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cells Demonstrate Effective In Vitro Killing Against DHG Cell Lines
paragraphs.text: We investigated the in vitro cytotoxic effect of LV-B7-H3 CAR-T cells against 2 DHG cell lines: KNS42 (H3G34V-mutated)-adherent cells and H3G34R-mutated (SJ-HGGX42) neurosphere cells. We employed different cytotoxicity assessment methods, that is, fluorescence-based assay using Celigo and Incucyte, and luminescence-based assay using a spectrophotometer. KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42 cells were cocultured with mock and B7-H3 CAR T cells at the indicated effector-to-target (B7-H3 CAR T: tumor cells) ratios for 72 h. In vitro killing revealed that B7-H3 CAR T cells had robust cytotoxicity, achieving near-complete eradication of tumor cells compared to mock T cells (Figure 3A–E). KNS42 cells (Figure 3A and B) demonstrated greater sensitivity to CAR T cell-mediated killing than SJ-HGGX42 (Figure 3D and E), supporting that CAR T cell efficacy correlates with B7-H3 expression on target tumor cells. Live-cell imaging revealed a marked reduction in viable KNS42 tumor cells following treatment with B7-H3 CAR T cells compared to mock T cells. At increasing E:T ratios (2:1 and 4:1), a substantial decrease in GFP-positive tumor cells was observed, consistent with enhanced tumor clearance. In contrast, mock T cells showed minimal cytotoxic effect, with abundant GFP-positive cells persisting across all conditions (Figure 3C).

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cells Demonstrate Effective In Vitro Killing Against DHG Cell Lines
paragraphs.text: We comprehensively evaluated the kinetics of B7-H3 CAR T cell-mediated cytotoxicity against KNS42 tumor cells across multiple effector-to-target (E:T) ratios (1:8, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 4:1) taking readings at every 8-h interval. A time and dose-dependent increase in tumor cell killing was observed compared to mock and CD19 CAR T cells at the 4:1 ratio. Higher E:T ratios (4:1) demonstrated rapid and near 80% tumor clearance beginning at 48-72 h postcoculture, whereas lower E:T ratios (1:8 and 1:4) showed slower and less efficient killing, with partial tumor cell killing even at 72 h (Figure S5A and B). These results indicate that both time and effector cell concentration critically influence the efficacy of B7-H3 CAR T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Additionally, to further investigate if B7-H3 CAR T cell cytotoxicity is dependent on antigen density on the target cells, we compared the cytotoxicity susceptibility of 2 neurosphere-forming glioma cell lines with differential B7-H3 expression: SJ-HGGX42 (low B7-H3) and OPBG-GBM001 (high B7-H3) (Figure 1C and D). At similar effector-to-target (E:T) ratios, we observed significantly greater cytotoxic activity of B7-H3 CAR T cells against OPBG-GBM001 relative to SJ-HGGX42 (Figure S6). Our data provide strong functional evidence that CAR T cell efficacy scales with B7-H3 expression on tumor cells. Similarly, 8H9-based retrovirus-B7-H3 CAR T cells also demonstrated significant killing potential against 2 DHG cell lines (KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42) (Figure S7A and B), further demonstrating the potential of B7-H3 CAR T cells as an effective strategy.

paragraphs.section: Results > Generation of B7-H3 Targeted CAR-T Cells
paragraphs.text: Following identification of 8H9 as the preferred antigen-binding domain based on its comparable antitumor activity and lower exhaustion profile relative to MGA271, we evaluated an alternative 8H9-based CAR configuration as a subsequent optimization strategy. This retrovirus-based second-generation B7-H3 CAR construct (RV-B7-H3 CAR T cells) incorporated the same 8H9 scFv but utilized a distinct backbone comprising a CD8α transmembrane region, a CD28 costimulatory domain, and a CD3α signaling domain (Figure S4A).30 Following CD3/CD28 stimulation, T cells exhibited activation marker expression (CD69, CD25, HLA-DR) and were successfully transduced with the RV-B7-H3 CAR construct, achieving ~60% surface CAR expression (Figure S4B and C). Proliferation assays on days 0, 4, and 8 showed no significant difference between CAR T and mock T cells, indicating that CAR expression did not impair T cell expansion (Figure S4D). Although both the 8H9 CAR constructs yielded similar killing efficacy (Figure S4E), CAR with CD4 transmembrane domain, 4-1BB costimulatory domain exhibited less exhaustion (Figure S4F). Collectively, these in vitro optimization studies established that CAR architecture, including the choice of scFv, transmembrane region, and costimulatory domain, substantially influences T cell fitness. Among the 3 B7-H3 CAR constructs evaluated, the 8H9-based CAR incorporating the CD4 transmembrane domain, 4-1BB costimulatory domain, and CD3ζ signaling domain exhibited the most favorable balance of cytotoxicity and reduced exhaustion. Therefore, this optimized construct was selected for all subsequent in vitro and in vivo studies in DHG model.

paragraphs.section: Results > Generation of B7-H3 Targeted CAR-T Cells
paragraphs.text: We designed a second-generation B7-H3 CAR construct using the B7-H3 scFv sequence derived from monoclonal antibodies 8H929,30 and MGA271.24,25 To generate B7-H3-directed CAR T cells, a humanized anti-B7-H3 (scFv), IgG4 hinge with EQ mutation, CD4 transmembrane domain,36,37 4-1BB costimulatory domain, and CD3ζ signaling domain (Figure 2A), was cloned into a lentiviral vector.37 The use of a 4-1BB costimulatory domain supports sustained CAR T cell persistence and reduced exhaustion, as previously demonstrated to promote memory formation and oxidative metabolism compared to CD28-based designs.38–41 This is particularly important for achieving durable responses in aggressive solid tumors such as DHG. Further, the selection of the IgG4 hinge/spacer was guided by comparative optimization studies that demonstrated enhanced antitumor activity and reduced exhaustion relative to CD8-based constructs (Figure S2). This highlights the importance of CAR structural design in balancing efficacy and T cell fitness. Human CD3+ T cells were activated with CD3/CD28 and then transduced with lentivirus containing the B7-H3 CAR construct, referred to as LV-B7-H3 CAR-T. The transduced T cells were checked for CAR expression by flow cytometry using antihuman IgG (Fcg fragment specific) after gating on the lymphocyte population, single and live cells (Figure 2B). We achieved ~45% B7-H3-positive CAR expression (Figure 2C). We next evaluated the basal exhaustion status of transduced T cells prior to antigen encounter. Surface expression of exhaustion markers 2B4, PD-1, Tim-3, and Lag-3 in B7-H3 CAR T cells was comparable to mock-transduced controls, indicating that CAR transduction alone did not induce premature T cell exhaustion (Figure 2D).

paragraphs.section: Results > B7-H3 CAR T Cell Did Not Affect the Viability of B7-H3 Negative Cells
paragraphs.text: To directly assess the antigen specificity of B7-H3 CAR T cell effector functions, we performed CRISPR-Cas9-based knockout (KO) of B7-H3 antigen in KNS42 and SJ-HGGX42 DHG cell lines and generated respective B7-H3KO cell lines. Flow cytometry and immunoblotting confirmed complete loss of B7-H3 surface and total protein expression in B7-H3KO cells (Figure 4A and B, Figure S9A–C). We observed a considerable loss of CAR T cells’ cytolytic activity against KNS42 B7-H3KO and SJ-HGGX42 B7-H3KO cells (Figure 4C, Figure S9D and E). B7-H3 CAR T cells showed no significant cytotoxicity against B7-H3KO KNS42 cells across E:T ratios up to 4:1, with tumor cell viability comparable to mock and CD19 CAR T cell controls, confirming target-specific activity (Figure 4D). Fluorescence imaging further confirmed the lack of B7-H3 CAR-mediated tumor killing in B7-H3KO cells, even at high E:T ratios (Figure 4E). Comparison of cytokine release after antigen stimulation revealed significant reduction by B7-H3KO cells compared to control cells (Figure 4F). Time-course analysis of B7-H3 CAR T cell cytotoxicity revealed that B7-H3 CAR T cells exhibited negligible cytotoxic activity against KNS42 B7-H3KO cells across all tested E:T ratios (1:8, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 4:1) over 72 h unlike parent KNS42 cells. Tumor cell viability remained unchanged throughout the assay, confirming the antigen-specific nature of B7-H3 CAR T cell-mediated killing and the requirement for B7-H3 expression on target cells (Figure S10). Further, to assess the dependence of CAR T cell activity on antigen availability/density, we performed a density-dependent cytotoxicity assay using mixed populations of B7-H3-positive and B7-H3KO KNS42 cell lines. B7-H3 CAR T cells demonstrated robust, antigen-dependent cytotoxicity that progressively decreased with declining proportions of B7-H3-positive targets and was completely abolished under antigen-negative conditions, whereas mock T cells showed no cytotoxicity across all conditions (Figure S11A). Lastly, we evaluated B7-H3 CAR T cell killing of B7-H3 negative TNBC cell line MDA-MB-453 and did not see any cytotoxicity (Figure S11B). Together, these results establish that B7-H3 CAR-T cell activation, cytotoxicity, and effector cytokine responses are strictly dependent on tumor-intrinsic B7-H3 expression, underscoring the high specificity and precision of this therapeutic strategy.

paragraphs.section: Discussion
paragraphs.text: B7-H3 CAR T cells were well tolerated, as we did not observe any evidence of toxicity after ICT delivery of B7-H3 CAR T cells in both DHG in vivo models (Figure S17). Our findings support the therapeutic advantages of local-regional intracranial delivery of B7-H3 CAR T cells, a strategy that bypasses the BBB and potentially minimizes systemic toxicity. Thus, preclinical studies suggest superior efficacy of locoregional delivery for B7-H3 CAR T cells and have demonstrated tumor regression in some models.47,48 Recent pediatric trials, including incorporated locoregional delivery, showed enhanced tumor penetration and reduced risks of cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, especially in DMG patients with preexisting neurological deficits.22,24 While locoregional delivery may reduce the incidence of systemic cytokine release syndrome, it does not eliminate the risk of neurotoxicity. Tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity and localized inflammatory effects remain important considerations following intracranial CAR T cell administration. In our models, comprehensive toxicity monitoring revealed no behavioral or neurological deficits following treatment, and histologic analysis demonstrated reduced microglial activation, consistent with resolution of tumor-associated inflammation rather than treatment-induced neurotoxicity (Figure 5G and H, Figure S14). In addition, serum cytokine profiling showed no evidence of severe systemic inflammatory responses (Figure S15D), supporting a favorable safety profile of B7-H3 CAR T therapy with locoregional delivery.19,20,28,49 The optimal route of CAR T cell delivery may depend on both anatomical tumor location and spatial distribution of the target antigen. Tumors located in surgically accessible cortical regions may be well suited for locoregional administration, whereas deep-seated or multifocal lesions may require alternative strategies. Importantly, antigen heterogeneity across primary and disseminated tumor sites can influence CAR T engagement and distribution, thereby impacting the effectiveness of localized vs systemic delivery approaches. Although we did not directly compare systemic vs intracranial administration, prior preclinical and clinical studies have demonstrated superior tumor control and CNS persistence with locoregional CAR T delivery in brain tumors.19,28 Given the cortical accessibility of DHG and emerging clinical evidence supporting intracranial approaches, we prioritized locoregional administration to enhance translational relevance. Consistent with prior preclinical and clinical studies,19,20,28,49 our findings support the therapeutic advantages of local-regional intracranial delivery of B7-H3 CAR T cells by enabling direct tumor targeting while bypassing the BBB. This approach achieved durable tumor clearance with minimal toxicity, likely driven by enhanced local effector activity and limited systemic exposure. Collaborative efforts are needed to optimize delivery routes and dosing regimens for B7-H3 targeted CAR T cell immunotherapies in pediatric CNS tumors.
